1.title: Secure and Govern Power BI
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Secure and Govern Power B I. It covers the exam area Manage and secure Power B I. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Assign workspace roles. Configure item-level access. Configure access to semantic models. Implement row-level security roles. Configure row-level security group membership. Apply sensitivity labels. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Manage and secure Power B I (fifteen-twenty percent). Exam format: a one hundred-minute proctored exam; a score of seven hundred on a scale to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official P L three hundred study guide, skills measured as of April twenty, twenty twenty-six.

1.title: Layers of protection: what protects what
1.text: Layers of protection: what protects what. Power B I security works in layers, and each layer protects a different thing. Many exam questions ask which layer fits. Read the requirement first, then name the layer, then pick the setting. One scenario can need two layers, for example row-level security for the rows and a sensitivity label for the exported file.

1.title: Layers of protection: what protects what, continued
1.text: Layers of protection: what protects what. The figure shows this: Row-level security gives each role its own rows of the same Sales table, so a West role and an East role see different data.

1.title: Layers of protection: what protects what, continued
1.text: Layers of protection: what protects what. Row-level security (R L S). What it protects: Rows of a semantic model. Where you set it: Roles in Desktop; members in the service. Who it applies to: Viewers only. Object-level security (O L S). What it protects: Columns and tables. Where you set it: Roles in the semantic model. Who it applies to: Members of the role. Workspace role. What it protects: Every item in the workspace. Where you set it: The workspace access list. Who it applies to: Users or groups.

1.title: Layers of protection: what protects what, continued
1.text: Layers of protection: what protects what. Item permission. What it protects: One item. Where you set it: Sharing or permissions of that item. Who it applies to: The people it is given to. Sensitivity label. What it protects: The content and its exports. Where you set it: Desktop or the service. Who it applies to: The labeled item and its downloads. Exam tip: R L S limits rows, O L S limits columns and tables, a role or permission decides what a person can do, and a label protects the file when it leaves. Match the layer to the verb in the question.

1.title: Workspace roles and item-level access
1.text: Workspace roles and item-level access. Admin. What it can do: Everything: delete the workspace, add or remove anyone, let Contributors update the app. Key limit: None. Member. What it can do: Add lower roles only, publish or update the app, share, edit content. Key limit: Cannot delete the workspace. Contributor. What it can do: Create, edit and delete content; schedule refresh. Key limit: Cannot publish an app (can update it only if an Admin allows). Viewer. What it can do: View and interact only. Key limit: The only role R L S applies to. Roles can be given to users or to groups.

1.title: Workspace roles and item-level access, continued
1.text: Workspace roles and item-level access. Item-level access is sharing one item. Sharing an item gives Read by default. The person gets that item only, not a place in the workspace. A workspace role reaches every item in the workspace; an item permission reaches one. Exam tip: A Contributor cannot publish an app, and only a Viewer is restricted by R L S. A Member can publish the app but cannot delete the workspace.

1.title: Access to semantic models
1.text: Access to semantic models. Read. Interact with reports built on the model. Build. Create new content from the model, Analyze in Excel, see hidden fields, export underlying data. Reshare. Give others access to the model. Write. Edit and republish the model. A workspace role brings these implicitly. Admin, Member. Read, Build, Reshare and Write. Contributor. Read, Build and Write. Viewer. Read only. Sharing gives Read by default. Build and Reshare are granted on purpose. Only the owner can change the scheduled refresh and credentials. Exam tip: Build lets people create new reports from a shared model; Read does not. A Viewer has Read only, so a Viewer needs Build granted to use Analyze in Excel.

1.title: Row-level security roles
1.text: Row-level security roles. R L S limits which rows a person sees. The steps are. In Desktop, on the Modeling tab, choose Manage roles. Create a role, pick a table and write a dacks filter. Test it with View as in Desktop or Test as role in the service. Publish, then add members in the service (section five). A static filter uses a fixed value, so you need one role per value. A dynamic filter uses user principal name, which returns the signed-in user's name, so one role serves everyone.

1.title: Row-level security roles, continued
1.text: Row-level security roles. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Row-level security roles, continued
1.text: Row-level security roles. Additive. A user in two roles sees the union of their rows. Who is limited. Viewers only, including Viewers with Build. Not limited. Admin, Member and Contributor (anyone with Write permission). Scope. Rows only; O L S covers columns and tables. Sources. Direct Query is supported. Exam tip: Define the role in Desktop, assign members in the service. If a Contributor still sees every row, R L S is not applied to that role.

1.title: RLS group membership and sensitivity labels
1.text: R L S group membership and sensitivity labels. Add members in the service: open the semantic model, then Security, choose the role and add users or groups. Security groups. Yes. Mail-enabled groups and distribution groups. Yes. Microsoft three sixty-five groups. No. Service principals. No.

2.title: RLS group membership and sensitivity labels, continued
2.text: R L S group membership and sensitivity labels. Sensitivity labels come from Microsoft Purview Information Protection. Apply in. Desktop (the Sensitivity button) and the service. Items. Semantic models, reports, dashboards, dataflows, paginated reports. Requirements. Pro or P P U, and membership of a security group allowed to apply labels. What it does. Does not control access in the service; it applies protection (encryption) on export to Excel, Power Point, P D F and.pbix download. Inheritance. New content inherits a label, and downstream content inherits too. Other. The more restrictive label wins on.pbix download; subscription attachments are protected. Exam tip: Microsoft three sixty-five groups are not supported for R L S membership; use a security group. A sensitivity label protects exports, it does not block viewing in the service.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A colleague must publish the workspace app and add people as Contributors, but must not be able to delete the workspace. Which role should the colleague get? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Member role on the workspace. A Member can publish the app and add lower roles but cannot delete the workspace, while an Admin can delete it and a Contributor cannot publish an app.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. An R L S role limits each sales region to its own rows. A user who is a workspace Contributor and is also assigned to a role still sees every row. What explains this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: R L S is applied only to users with the Viewer role. R L S is not applied to Admin, Member or Contributor, because they have Write permission on the model.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Each sales rep must see only their own customers, and the Customer table has an Email column. There are three hundred reps. What is the best design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A dynamic role that compares Email with the signed-in user. One dynamic role with user principal name serves every rep, while static roles would need three hundred roles.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. An admin wants to add a whole team to an R L S role by using one group in the service. Which group can be added? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A security group of the team members. Security groups are supported for R L S membership, while Microsoft three sixty-five groups and service principals are not.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A user must build new reports from a shared semantic model but must not change or republish it. Which permission should the user get on the model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Build permission on the semantic model. Build allows creating new content from the model, while Write would allow editing and republishing it.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A report labeled Confidential is exported to Power Point by an analyst. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: The exported file keeps the label and its protection. Sensitivity labels apply protection to exports such as Excel, Power Point and P D F files.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which workspace role can delete the workspace? Answer: Admin. Question two. Which role is the only one that R L S restricts? Answer: Viewer. Question three. Where do you define R L S roles, and where do you add members? Answer: Roles in Desktop on the Modeling tab; members in the service under the model's Security.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which dacks function returns the signed-in user's name for dynamic R L S? Answer: user principal name. Question five. What access does sharing an item give by default? Answer: Read. Question six. Which security hides columns and tables rather than rows? Answer: Object-level security.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. What protects what: R L S rows; O L S columns and tables; workspace role all items; item permission one item. Workspace roles: Admin everything; Member adds lower roles and publishes the app. Item-level access: sharing gives Read by default; item permission is narrower than a role. Model permissions: Read, Build, Reshare, Write; Admin and Member all four; Contributor three; Viewer Read. R L S roles: Desktop, Modeling, Manage roles; static or dynamic with user principal name; additive; Viewers only. R L S membership: service, model, Security; security, mail-enabled and distribution groups yes. Sensitivity labels: Microsoft Purview Information Protection; Desktop and service; Pro or P P U; encrypt on export; inheritance.
